summary: The audience is built to share Hamlet's doubt and disgust, to wait with mounting suspense for the act he delays, and to grieve the pile of dead.

need-to-breathe.why: Nothing is built to affect the audience's breath.

hungry.why: Nothing is built to produce hunger.

full.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

thirsty.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

gassy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-poop.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-pee.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

sleepy.why: The play does not aim to lull its audience.

nauseous.why: Nothing is built to sicken the audience.

urge-to-sneeze.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

urge-to-cough.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

dizzy.why: Nothing is built to produce vertigo.

fatigued.why: The audience is not made to feel bodily exertion.

pain.why: The poisoned wounds and Gertrude's death are built for a wince, no more.

disgusted.why: Hamlet's images of the enseamed bed, the unweeded garden, and the rotting Yorick are built to make the audience share his revulsion.

itchy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

tickled.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

over-stimulated.why: Nothing is built to overwhelm the senses.

too-hot-too-cold.why: The bitter cold of the battlements is atmosphere, not built to chill the audience.

afraid.why: The Ghost's entrances at midnight are built to frighten, the play opening as a ghost story.

anxious.why: The audience dreads what Hamlet will do, what Claudius plans, and what will become of Ophelia, a dread the play prolongs.

panic.why: Nothing is built to produce panic in the audience.

sensory-pleasures.why: Nothing is built to give the audience sensory pleasure.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The soliloquies, the wordplay, and the players' speeches are the richest language in English drama, built for the audience's delight in words.

piquancy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

fun-excitement.why: The fencing match and the play-within-the-play are built as exciting spectacle.

orgasm.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

love-romantic.why: Hamlet's letters and his outburst at Ophelia's grave are built to make the audience feel a love that was real and wasted.

love-family.why: The Ghost's appeal to his son and Laertes' grief for Polonius and Ophelia are built to touch family feeling.

grief.why: Ophelia's mad scene and drowning, and Horatio's farewell to his sweet prince, are built to make the audience mourn.

missing-someone.why: Hamlet's longing for his father gives the audience a moment of felt absence.

aroused-sexually.why: Hamlet's bawdy talk to Ophelia is built for discomfort, not arousal.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The audience is built to love Horatio as the one steady friend, and to like Hamlet through his wit.

empathy.why: The soliloquies put the audience inside Hamlet's mind for whole speeches, so his doubt and self-reproach become the audience's own.

compassion.why: Ophelia's madness and Hamlet's trapped grief are built to produce pity.

grateful.why: Nothing is built to make the audience grateful.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

trustful-distrustful.why: The audience hears Claudius confess at prayer and watches the spying, so it knows whom to distrust while Hamlet still doubts.

depressed.why: Hamlet's melancholy soliloquies can lower the audience's mood, which the play intends in measure.

angry.why: Claudius's murder and Polonius's manipulation of Ophelia are built to anger the audience.

envious.why: Nothing is built to produce envy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Nothing is built to make the audience jealous.

jealous-friendship.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

hatred.why: Claudius is built to be hated once his guilt is confirmed, though his prayer complicates it.

contempt.why: Polonius's platitudes, Osric's affectations, and Rosencrantz and Guildenstern's servility are built for the audience's scorn.

resentment.why: The audience feels the injustice of Claudius's usurpation and of Ophelia's grudging burial.

proud.why: Nothing is built to make the audience proud.

amused.why: The gravedigger, Polonius's windiness, Osric, and Hamlet's puns are built for laughter in a tragedy.

sense-of-belonging.why: The audience is not recruited to a side; Denmark is everyone's prison.

lonely.why: Hamlet confiding only in the audience makes it share his isolation at court.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The play is built to make the audience weigh revenge, suicide, and incest, and judge Claudius, Gertrude, and Hamlet's cruelty to Ophelia.

admiration.why: Hamlet's wit and Horatio's constancy are built to be admired, and the players' art within the play.

embarrassed.why: Ophelia squirming at Hamlet's public bawdry gives the audience secondhand embarrassment.

shame.why: The audience feels Hamlet's self-contempt from within but is not shamed.

guilt.why: Nothing is built to make the audience guilty.

sad.why: From the inky cloak to the bodies on the stage, the play is built to produce sorrow.

happy.why: Nothing is built to make the audience content.

joyful-euphoric.why: The Mousetrap's success gives the audience a brief surge with Hamlet.

effort.why: The play's length and dense verse ask persistence of an audience, though less than reading it does.

focused-in-flow.why: The Mousetrap, the closet scene, and the duel are built to hold the audience rapt.

bored.why: Hamlet's delay can test a restless audience, but the play aims at tension, not tedium.

impatient.why: The audience is built to feel Hamlet's delay as its own impatience, speech after speech, until the duel.

curious.why: Is the Ghost honest, is Hamlet mad, what will he do: the play is built around the audience's questions.

surprised.why: The Ghost's revelation, Polonius stabbed behind the arras, and the final carnage are built to startle.

awe.why: The Ghost in armor and Hamlet's speech on what a piece of work is a man are built to produce wonder.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The audience is made to share Hamlet's doubt of the Ghost and to doubt his sanity, Ophelia's honesty, and Claudius's repentance.

feeling-of-knowing.why: Nothing is built to make a clue almost land for the audience.

confused.why: Whether Hamlet's madness is feigned and why he delays are left open, so a first-time audience is meant to be unsure.

frustrated.why: The audience is built to feel the frustration of Hamlet's delay, especially when he spares Claudius at prayer.

uncertain-certain.why: The play is built to keep the audience uncertain of Hamlet's mind and of the ending until the last scene.

understanding.why: Hamlet's readiness is all is built to give the audience the play's understanding before the end.

inspired.why: The soliloquies are built to provoke thought in the audience about death, action, and conscience.

satisfied.why: Claudius dies by his own poison and the stage is cleared for Fortinbras, closing the revenge at the cost of all.

foreboding.why: Something is rotten in Denmark, the Ghost walks, and Hamlet feels ill about his heart before the duel; the play is built on dread.

nostalgia.why: Yorick's skull and Hamlet's memory of his father give the audience a backward ache.

anticipation-suspense.why: The audience waits for the Ghost, watches Claudius's face during the play, and knows the foil is poisoned before Hamlet does.

hope.why: The audience hopes Hamlet will act and that Ophelia will be spared, hopes the play builds to deny.

schadenfreude.why: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern hoist with their own petard and Claudius forced to drink his poison are built to be enjoyed.

elevation.why: Horatio's loyalty and the dying exchange of forgiveness are built to lift the audience briefly.

infatuation.why: Hamlet's letters to Ophelia are observed, not shared.

rage.why: Laertes' storming of the palace carries a flash of rage to the audience.
